planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Labyrinth is a large formal decorative dahlia producing warm blush-to-orange blooms that shift in tone across the flower, a popular cut-flower variety alongside Café au Lait among floral designers. Stake plants early since the heavy blooms on tall stems require support.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake immediately. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage branching and more blooms per plant. Labyrinth is a large formal decorative dahlia bearing full, densely petaled blooms that open a soft peachy-blush at the center and deepen toward warm orange-apricot tones at the outer petals, a complex, layered coloring that has made it a favorite alongside Café au Lait among wedding and cut-flower growers seeking warm, muted tones. Blooms run 6-8 inches across on strong stems well suited to cutting, and the plant produces continuously from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading and harvesting. In zone 9, peak summer heat can dull flower color and reduce bloom size somewhat, with the best color and largest blooms typically appearing in the cooler weather of early summer and fall. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

common_name: Kelvin Floodlight Dahlia (Giant Golden-Yellow Dinnerplate Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Kelvin Floodlight is a classic giant dinnerplate dahlia producing enormous, clear golden-yellow blooms on tall, sturdy plants, one of the most widely grown large-flowered exhibition and garden dahlias. Stake plants early since the very heavy blooms require support.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake immediately, since Kelvin Floodlight produces some of the largest blooms of any commonly grown dahlia. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant. A longtime favorite in exhibition and garden circles, Kelvin Floodlight bears massive, clear golden-yellow, informal decorative blooms that can reach 10-12 inches across on strong, tall stems, giving it a genuinely dramatic presence in the summer and fall border. Its bright, pure yellow color holds up well through the season compared to some of the more subtly toned modern dahlia varieties, providing reliable, bold color from midsummer to frost with regular deadheading. Because the flowers are so large and heavy, disbudding side buds to focus energy into fewer, larger blooms is common practice for exhibition-quality flowers, though leaving buds intact still produces an impressive garden display. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Penhill Watermelon is a ball-type dahlia producing perfectly round, densely petaled blooms in a vivid rose-watermelon pink, valued by cut-flower growers for its neat form and excellent vase life.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants for support as they grow. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage branching and increase the number of blooms. Penhill Watermelon is a ball dahlia, a form characterized by perfectly spherical, densely and evenly packed blooms roughly 3-4 inches across, in a bright, saturated rose-pink reminiscent of watermelon flesh that holds its color well through the season. The tidy, uniform bloom shape and mid-sized flower make it especially popular with cut-flower growers and floral designers, since ball dahlias hold their form and color exceptionally well in the vase, often lasting a week or more after cutting. Plants are relatively compact compared to giant dinnerplate types, making them useful in mixed borders as well as dedicated cutting gardens. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the plant producing from midsummer through frost. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

common_name: American Dawn Dahlia (Large Coral-Pink Dinnerplate Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; American Dawn is a large informal decorative dahlia bearing bold coral-pink blooms with a soft golden blush at the center, a popular large-flowered garden and cut-flower variety. Stake plants early since the heavy blooms on tall stems require support.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake immediately. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant. American Dawn is a large informal decorative dahlia producing bold, coral-pink blooms 8-9 inches across, with petals that soften toward a warm golden-peach glow near the center, giving the flower noticeable depth and dimension compared to single-toned varieties. The tall, vigorous plants produce continuously from midsummer through the first hard frost with regular deadheading, and the large, sturdy-stemmed blooms make excellent cut flowers. In zone 9, provide afternoon shade or expect some fading of the coral coloring during the most intense summer heat, with the richest color typically appearing in spring and fall. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

common_name: Totally Tangerine Dahlia (Single Collarette-Type Orange Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Totally Tangerine is an award-winning single/collarette-type dahlia with airy, semi-double burnt-orange blooms on tall, branching stems, prized by pollinator gardeners and cut-flower growers alike for its open, bee-accessible flower form.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants as they grow. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage branching. Totally Tangerine bears distinctive, semi-double, burnt-orange blooms with a prominent open center and slightly twisted, waterlily-like petals, a looser, airier flower form than the fully double blooms of most decorative and ball dahlias. That open center makes the flower's pollen and nectar accessible to bees and butterflies, which most fully double dahlia forms block entirely, making Totally Tangerine one of the more pollinator-friendly dahlia choices without sacrificing garden impact. It won the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its outstanding, prolific, long-season bloom on strong, well-branched plants that need less disbudding and staking effort than giant dinnerplate types. Deadhead regularly to keep the plant flowering continuously from midsummer through the first frost. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.
